name: Lenakel
catalog_quote: In phrases and sentences, each word maintains its own internal stress pattern, but primary stress occurs only once in the string. Thus the last primary-stressed vowel retains primary stress, while all other occurrences of primary stress reduce to secondary stress, and all occurrences of secondary stress reduce to tertiary stress

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (penultimate primary stress; drop from the strict set), or keep with word-class-split grids: verbs/adjectives stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 10010 101010 1010010 (1 = a stressed syllable), nouns/adjuncts stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 101010 0101010 (1 = a stressed syllable) The strict set is defined as 'one weight-blind rule with no rule-level exceptions'; Lynch 1978:19 / 1974:181-184 state two secondary-stress rules by word class (diverging at 5 and 7 syllables, the coded grid being the verb one only), plus rule-level final primary stress for words ending in VV(C), glide+C, glide+h and for the clitic -ɨn (1978:19-20; 1974:188-202), and ~15 lexical antepenults (1974:218). If the catalog counts Lynch's 'penultimate vowel' (mora-counting) formulation as weight-blind, primary-stress position alone could stay fixed: penultimate syllable in the dominant set; the single secondary grid cannot stand as strict.

audit.reasoning: (1) No deciding quote in the record; the Lynch 1978 passages named in refs/the domain locator are verbatim in the held at book p.19 (the domain locator's 'p.20' for the domain quote is off by one). (2) The classification rests on StressTyp2's 2015 coding; the primary descriptions are Lynch 1978 (held) and Lynch 1974 (downloaded now, open, ScholarSpace) — the best and only descriptions per Glottolog and a Crossref check; (3) Both primary sources, on pages opened here, give penultimate primary stress but two direction-opposed secondary-stress rules split by word class, regular final-stress classes (underlying geminate vowels, glide+C, -ɨn), and a small lexical antepenult class; the record's single grid is the verb pattern only and its 'strict' flag conflicts with the catalog's own

sources.quote: Primary stress on the penultimate vowel (monosyllables stressed); verbs and adjectives take initial plus rightward-alternating secondary stress (never on the pretonic), nouns and adjuncts take leftward-alternating secondary stress from the penult; surface final stress arises regularly from underlying geminate vowels, the = boundary and glide re-formation; ~15 lexically marked antepenults; one primary stress per phrase (rightmost word).
sources.locator: ch. V 'Stress', pp.181-222: §5.1 p.181-182 ('With a very few exceptions.. primary stress in Lenakel is assigned to the penultimate vowel.. Lenakel is rather unusual in having two rules of alternating stress which apply in different directions. In Lenakel nouns, secondary stress occurs on alternate syllables to the left of the primary stress. Secondary stresses in verbs, however, are found on the initial syllable and alternate syllables to the right'); §5.1.1 pp.182-184 rules (3) PRIMARY STRESS ASSIGNMENT, (5) LEFTWARD ALTERNATING STRESS (nouns/adjuncts), (6) INITIAL STRESS (verbs/adjectives); §5.1.2 p.188 boundary = gives final stress; §5.1.3 pp.192-193 final stress from underlying geminate vowel clusters (asíis 'to swell up', amnúum 'to drink', kapáas 'axe'); §5.3 pp.218-221 about fifteen lexical items with antepenultimate primary stress (hospital, sikaret, polisman..), 'about half of one percent of the lexical items'; summary p.8-9 of ch. I.
sources.note: The only full phonology of Lenakel (Glottolog's top-ranked item), with a 40-page stress chapter giving the explicit noun-vs-verb secondary-stress rules, the regular final-stress classes and the count of lexical exceptions that decide whether this record belongs in the strict set; downloaded now.
